strategy_title: Adding maxnreg=128 to Large-Tile Configs Causes Cache Collapse
strategy_description: Adding maxnreg=128 to all autotune configs (keeping BLOCK_M=256, block_size=256) successfully doubled theoretical occupancy from 12.5% to 25% and reduced registers/thread from 255 to 128, but caused a catastrophic 2.1x regression in kernel duration (9.9ms → 20.94ms). The root cause is that capping registers with maxnreg forces the compiler to spill live values to the stack/local memory, collapsing L1/TEX hit rate from 35.8% to 10.4% and L2 hit rate from 92.7% to 65.5%, while DRAM throughput exploded from 22.8% to 58.3%. Warp Cycles Per Issued Instruction jumped from 8.05 to 29.35 cycles (3.6x worse), and the CPIStall rule reported L1TEX stalls consuming 72.6% of cycles (21.3 cycles/warp average, up from 3.0 cycles). The additional warps from improved occupancy could not hide the dramatically longer memory latency caused by spill traffic — the no-eligible-warp percentage actually worsened from 75.2% to 86.5% despite more active warps, because all warps were simultaneously stalled on spill loads/stores.
applicable_when: Never applicable as described — this is a negative example. Adding maxnreg to large-tile configs (BLOCK_M=256) when the kernel body contains tl.static_range unrolled loops (KH*KW=9 bodies) causes this regression.
do_not_apply_when: Do not add maxnreg constraints to autotune configs when the kernel body contains tl.static_range unrolled outer loops (e.g., KERNEL_H x KERNEL_W = 9 unrolled bodies) with large tile sizes (BLOCK_M >= 128). The unrolled loop bodies require many simultaneously live register values; capping registers forces the compiler to spill these to local memory, collapsing L1/TEX hit rate (35% → 10%), exploding DRAM throughput (23% → 58%), and causing Warp Cycles Per Issued Instruction to jump 3-4x. The occupancy improvement from maxnreg is completely overwhelmed by spill traffic. This anti-pattern is especially severe when: (1) the kernel already has tl.static_range unrolling of spatial loops, (2) BLOCK_M is large (≥128), and (3) the stack size grows significantly after adding maxnreg.
framework_notes: In Triton, maxnreg in triton.Config caps the register file per thread, but when the kernel's live value set exceeds this cap (due to tl.static_range unrolling creating many simultaneously live [BLOCK_M]-sized vectors), the compiler spills to local memory (stack). The stack size grew from 1120 to 2464 bytes after adding maxnreg=128, confirming heavy spilling. The waves_per_sm halved (244 → 122) because the grid_size was unchanged but the autotuner selected a config that ran fewer waves. The key diagnostic signal is: if adding maxnreg causes stack_size to grow by >50%, the spill penalty will dominate any occupancy benefit.

strategy_title: Switching tl.static_range to range() Fails to Fix Spill Regression
strategy_description: Replacing tl.static_range with range() for the outer kh/kw loops successfully reduced registers/thread from 255 to 128 and improved theoretical occupancy from 12.5% to 25%, but the kernel still regressed vs. the flat-K-loop baseline (9.9ms → 7.6ms, only 0.61x speedup relative to the baseline). The local load/store spill signature (1.0/32 bytes per sector) persisted in the after profile, and uncoalesced global access worsened (excessive sectors grew from 47% to 60% of total sectors, 138M → 268M excessive sectors). The instruction count also increased (1.76B → 2.03B). The nested kh/kw/in_c loop structure itself — regardless of whether tl.static_range or range() is used — produces worse memory access patterns than the flat K-loop baseline, because the NHWC input pointer arithmetic (x_spatial[:, None] + offs_ic[None, :]) generates strided, uncoalesced global loads that the flat K-loop's modulo/division decode does not. The occupancy improvement from removing tl.static_range is real but insufficient to overcome the structural access pattern penalty of the nested loop formulation.
slow_pseudocode:
# BEFORE (this iteration's starting point): tl.static_range, 255 regs, 9.9ms
for kh_idx in tl.static_range(KERNEL_H):   # full unroll, 255 regs/thread
    for kw_idx in tl.static_range(KERNEL_W):
        ih = out_h + kh_idx
        iw = out_w + kw_idx
        x_spatial = base_x_m + ih * stride_xh + iw * stride_xw
        for ic_off in range(0, IN_C, BLOCK_K):
            x_ptrs = x_spatial[:, None] + offs_ic[None, :] * stride_xc
            acc = tl.dot(x_tile, w_tile, acc=acc)
fast_pseudocode:
# AFTER: range() instead of tl.static_range, 128 regs, 7.6ms — still slower than flat-K baseline
for kh_idx in range(KERNEL_H):   # no unroll, 128 regs/thread
    for kw_idx in range(KERNEL_W):
        ih = out_h + kh_idx
        iw = out_w + kw_idx
        x_spatial = base_x_m + ih * stride_xh + iw * stride_xw
        for ic_off in range(0, IN_C, BLOCK_K):
            x_ptrs = x_spatial[:, None] + offs_ic[None, :] * stride_xc
            acc = tl.dot(x_tile, w_tile, acc=acc)
applicable_when: Never applicable as described — this is a negative example. The nested kh/kw/in_c loop structure for NHWC convolution produces worse uncoalesced global access than the flat K-loop baseline regardless of whether tl.static_range or range() is used for the outer loops.
do_not_apply_when: Do not use nested kh/kw/in_c loops for NHWC implicit-GEMM convolution when the flat K-loop baseline already achieves good L1 hit rate (>60%) and low warp stall cycles (<7 cycles/instruction). The nested loop formulation generates strided x_spatial[:, None] + offs_ic[None, :] pointer arithmetic that causes uncoalesced global loads (60% excessive sectors), which cannot be fixed by simply switching tl.static_range to range(). The flat K-loop with inline modulo/division decode is structurally superior for coalesced access in NHWC layout.
framework_notes: In Triton, switching from tl.static_range to range() for outer loops does reduce register pressure (255 → 128 regs/thread) and improve occupancy (12.5% → 25%), but this is only beneficial if the underlying memory access pattern is sound. When the nested loop structure itself causes uncoalesced global loads (UncoalescedGlobalAccess rule: 60% excessive sectors), the occupancy improvement is insufficient to compensate. The local load/store spill signature (1.0/32 bytes per sector from MemoryCacheAccessPattern) persisted even after the tl.static_range → range() change, suggesting the spill source shifted but was not eliminated — likely due to the increased instruction count (2.03B vs 1.76B) and the autotune selecting a different config (block_size=128, grid=64516 vs block_size=256, grid=32258).

strategy_title: Weight Pre-Transpose for Coalescing Has No Effect on Flat K-Loop
strategy_description: Pre-transposing the weight tensor from [OUT_C, IN_C, KH, KW] to [KH, KW, IN_C, OUT_C] before the kernel launch (and updating stride parameters accordingly) produced essentially no change in any profiling metric: duration moved from 7.6ms to 7.5ms (within noise), excessive sectors remained at 268M (60% of total), L1/TEX hit rate was unchanged at ~25%, and Warp Cycles Per Issued Instruction barely moved (10.55 → 10.45). The uncoalesced global access rule still fired with identical severity, indicating the weight layout change did not affect the actual memory access pattern. The likely cause is that the flat K-loop's weight pointer arithmetic — which uses runtime stride parameters — was already generating the same effective access pattern regardless of the physical layout, or the diff was empty (no code change was actually applied). When the dominant uncoalesced access source is not the weight tensor but rather the input activation (NHWC strided loads) or local spill traffic, transposing the weight layout cannot address the bottleneck.
slow_pseudocode:
# BEFORE: weight layout [OUT_C, IN_C, KH, KW]
w = p_conv_weight.contiguous()
stride_wco = w.stride(0)  # = IN_C*KH*KW = 72
stride_wci = w.stride(1)  # = KH*KW = 9
stride_wkh = w.stride(2)  # = KW = 3
stride_wkw = w.stride(3)  # = 1
# kernel: w_ptrs = W_ptr + offs_n*stride_wco + in_c*stride_wci + kh*stride_wkh + kw*stride_wkw
fast_pseudocode:
# AFTER (no effect): weight layout [KH, KW, IN_C, OUT_C]
w = p_conv_weight.permute(2, 3, 1, 0).contiguous()
stride_wkh = w.stride(0)  # = KW*IN_C*OUT_C
stride_wkw = w.stride(1)  # = IN_C*OUT_C
stride_wci = w.stride(2)  # = OUT_C = 64
stride_wco = w.stride(3)  # = 1
# kernel body unchanged — same uncoalesced access pattern observed
applicable_when: Never applicable as described — this is a negative example. Pre-transposing the weight tensor when the kernel uses a flat K-loop with runtime stride parameters does not change the observed memory access pattern or reduce excessive sectors.
do_not_apply_when: Do not apply weight pre-transposition as a fix for UncoalescedGlobalAccess when: (1) the profiling diff shows no change in excessive sectors after the layout change, (2) the flat K-loop uses runtime stride parameters (stride_wco, stride_wci) that are already passed correctly, and (3) the local load/store spill signature (1.0/32 bytes per sector) persists — indicating the dominant uncoalesced traffic is from register spills, not weight loads. In this kernel, the 268M excessive sectors and 25% L1/TEX hit rate are driven by NHWC input activation loads and spill traffic, not weight layout. Transposing the weight tensor cannot fix these sources.
framework_notes: The unified diff was empty, suggesting the code change may not have been applied at all, or the kernel's runtime stride parameters already adapted to the new layout without any observable effect. In Triton, when weight strides are passed as kernel arguments (not compile-time constants), the compiler cannot specialize the access pattern at compile time — the hardware memory coalescing behavior depends on the actual runtime stride values. If the diff was truly empty, this is an implementation_flaw rather than a strategy failure, but the profiling shows the before/after kernels are nearly identical, making the distinction moot for learning purposes.

strategy_title: Flat K-Loop with constexpr IN_C Collapses Occupancy via Register Explosion
strategy_description: Switching from a nested kh/kw/in_c loop (range(), 128 regs/thread, 25% occupancy) to a flat K-loop with IN_C declared as tl.constexpr caused registers/thread to jump from 128 to 255, collapsing theoretical occupancy from 25% to 12.5% and Block Limit Registers from 4 to 2. Although duration improved from 7.6ms to 5.35ms (the flat K-loop is structurally better), the kernel is still slower than the historical flat-K baseline of 4.81ms because the constexpr IN_C declaration allows the compiler to aggressively unroll or specialize the modulo/division decode, inflating register pressure. The key diagnostic: declaring IN_C as tl.constexpr in a flat K-loop that uses `offs_k % IN_C` and `offs_k // IN_C` enables compile-time specialization that increases register demand, pushing the kernel into the same register-limited regime (255 regs, 12.5% occupancy) seen in prior regressions, even though the loop structure itself is correct.
fast_pseudocode:
# AFTER: flat K-loop, IN_C: tl.constexpr, TOTAL_K: tl.constexpr, 255 regs, 12.5% occupancy, 5.35ms
# IN_C declared constexpr causes register explosion via compile-time specialization
TOTAL_K: tl.constexpr = KERNEL_H * KERNEL_W * IN_C
for k_off in range(0, TOTAL_K, BLOCK_K):
    offs_k = k_off + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_K)
    in_c = offs_k % IN_C       # constexpr IN_C enables aggressive unrolling
    kw_idx = (offs_k // IN_C) % KERNEL_W
    kh_idx = offs_k // (IN_C * KERNEL_W)
    ih = out_h[:, None] + kh_idx[None, :]
    iw = out_w[:, None] + kw_idx[None, :]
    acc = tl.dot(x_tile, w_tile, acc=acc, allow_tf32=True)
applicable_when: Never applicable as described — this is a negative example. The flat K-loop structure is correct, but declaring IN_C as tl.constexpr when IN_C is large (e.g., 64+) causes register explosion in the modulo/division decode path.
do_not_apply_when: Do not declare IN_C as tl.constexpr in a flat K-loop that uses `offs_k % IN_C` and `offs_k // IN_C` arithmetic. The constexpr annotation allows the Triton compiler to specialize and potentially unroll the decode logic, inflating registers/thread from 128 to 255 and collapsing theoretical occupancy from 25% to 12.5%. Additionally, do not compute TOTAL_K as a tl.constexpr derived from constexpr IN_C, KERNEL_H, KERNEL_W — this causes the loop trip count to be compile-time known, enabling further unrolling. Keep IN_C as a runtime parameter (no constexpr) in the flat K-loop formulation. The historical flat-K baseline at 4.81ms used IN_C as a runtime parameter.
framework_notes: In Triton, declaring a parameter as tl.constexpr allows the compiler to specialize the kernel at compile time, which can enable loop unrolling and constant folding. When TOTAL_K is also computed as tl.constexpr (TOTAL_K: tl.constexpr = KERNEL_H * KERNEL_W * IN_C), the flat K-loop's trip count becomes compile-time known, and the compiler may unroll the entire loop or aggressively specialize the modulo/division decode, dramatically increasing register demand. The autotune also selected a config with 3x more shared memory (24.58 KB → 73.73 KB per block), which reduced Block Limit Shared Mem from 5 to 3 — a secondary contributor to the occupancy collapse. The correct flat K-loop formulation should pass IN_C as a runtime parameter (not constexpr) and compute TOTAL_K at runtime.

strategy_title: Small Tiles + range() Loops Explode Grid Size and Instruction Count
strategy_description: Switching from large-tile configs (BLOCK_M=128-256) to exclusively small-tile configs (BLOCK_M<=64) combined with replacing tl.static_range with range() for outer kh/kw loops reduced registers/thread from 255 to 228 but failed to improve occupancy (still 12.5%, Block Limit Registers still 2). The dominant regression cause was a 4x increase in grid size (64516 → 258064 blocks) driven by smaller BLOCK_M tiles, which multiplied total executed instructions by 3.1x (1.68B → 5.16B), increasing kernel duration from 5.35ms to 13.5ms (0.34x speedup). Although L1/TEX hit rate improved dramatically (23% → 86%) due to better data reuse within smaller tiles, and warp stall cycles improved slightly (4.49 → 3.72 cycles/instruction), the sheer volume of additional work from the 4x larger grid overwhelmed all other gains. The structural anti-pattern is: reducing BLOCK_M to recover occupancy when the kernel is already register-limited by factors other than tile size causes grid explosion that multiplies total work without proportionally improving per-block efficiency.
slow_pseudocode:
# BEFORE: large tiles, flat K-loop, 255 regs, grid=64516, 5.35ms
@triton.autotune(configs=[
    Config(BLOCK_M=128, BLOCK_N=64, BLOCK_K=32, num_stages=3, num_warps=4),
    Config(BLOCK_M=64,  BLOCK_N=64, BLOCK_K=32, num_stages=3, num_warps=4),
    ...
])
for k_off in range(0, TOTAL_K, BLOCK_K):  # flat K-loop
    in_c = offs_k % IN_C
    kh = (offs_k // IN_C) % KERNEL_W
    kw = offs_k // (IN_C * KERNEL_W)
    acc = tl.dot(x_tile, w_tile, acc=acc)  # 255 regs, grid=64516, 1.68B inst
applicable_when: Never applicable as described — this is a negative example. Reducing BLOCK_M to small tiles (<=64) when the kernel is already register-limited (Block Limit Registers=2) causes grid explosion without recovering occupancy.
do_not_apply_when: Do not reduce BLOCK_M to small tiles (<=64) as an occupancy recovery strategy when Block Limit Registers is already >=2 and the register count is near 255. If the kernel's theoretical occupancy is already capped by register pressure at 12.5% and Block Limit Registers=2, reducing tile size will not improve occupancy (the register count per thread remains high at 228) but will multiply grid size by 4x, increasing total instruction count by 3x and causing severe duration regression. The signal that this strategy will fail: after applying small tiles, if registers/thread remains above 200 and Block Limit Registers remains at 2, the grid explosion dominates. Additionally, do not use this strategy when the nested kh/kw/in_c loop structure is retained — the combination of small tiles + nested loops produces 5.16B instructions vs 1.68B for the large-tile flat-K baseline.
framework_notes: In Triton, the grid size is determined by ceil(M_TOTAL / BLOCK_M) * ceil(OUT_C / BLOCK_N) * BATCH. Reducing BLOCK_M from 128 to 32 quadruples the grid size, which multiplies total kernel work proportionally. The autotuner selected BLOCK_M=32 from the small-tile config space, producing grid=258064 vs the prior grid=64516. The L1/TEX hit rate improvement (23% → 86%) from smaller tiles is real but insufficient to compensate for 3x more total instructions. The waves_per_sm metric (244 → 977) confirms the grid explosion: 977 waves means each SM must process ~7.4 waves sequentially, adding substantial scheduling overhead. The nested range() loop structure also contributed to the instruction count increase vs the flat K-loop formulation.

strategy_title: num_stages=1 + Larger BLOCK_M Configs Collapse Occupancy Further
strategy_description: Replacing autotune configs (num_stages=2/3) with all num_stages=1 configs while simultaneously introducing larger BLOCK_M=256 options caused the autotuner to select a 256-thread block config, pushing Block Limit Registers from 2 to 1 and Block Limit Shared Mem from 3 to 1, worsening no-eligible-warp cycles from 56% to 76% and nearly doubling kernel duration (5.35ms → 10.08ms). Registers/thread remained at 255 in both cases, confirming that reducing num_stages did not reduce register pressure — the dominant effect was the autotuner selecting a larger-block config that saturated both register and shared memory limits simultaneously. The structural anti-pattern is: when a kernel is already register-limited at 255 regs/thread, adding larger BLOCK_M configs to the autotune search space without a register cap will cause the autotuner to select the larger config, further collapsing Block Limit Registers and Block Limit Shared Mem, worsening occupancy even if num_stages is reduced.
slow_pseudocode:
# BEFORE: flat K-loop, num_stages=2/3, block_size=128, 12.5% occupancy, 5.35ms
@triton.autotune(configs=[
    Config(BLOCK_M=128, BLOCK_N=64, BLOCK_K=32, num_stages=3, num_warps=4),
    Config(BLOCK_M=128, BLOCK_N=64, BLOCK_K=16, num_stages=2, num_warps=4),
    Config(BLOCK_M=64,  BLOCK_N=64, BLOCK_K=32, num_stages=3, num_warps=4),
    ...
])
for k_off in range(0, TOTAL_K, BLOCK_K):
    in_c = offs_k % IN_C
    kw_idx = (offs_k // IN_C) % KERNEL_W
    kh_idx = offs_k // (IN_C * KERNEL_W)
    acc = tl.dot(x_tile, w_tile, acc=acc, allow_tf32=True)  # 255 regs, block=128, 5.35ms
applicable_when: Never applicable as described — this is a negative example. Reducing num_stages to 1 while adding larger BLOCK_M configs causes the autotuner to select a register-heavy, large-block config that worsens occupancy.
do_not_apply_when: Do not set num_stages=1 and simultaneously introduce larger BLOCK_M configs (e.g., BLOCK_M=256, num_warps=8) when the kernel is already at 255 registers/thread. The autotuner will select the larger config, pushing Block Limit Registers and Block Limit Shared Mem both to 1, halving the already-low occupancy. Additionally, do not reintroduce tl.static_range for outer kh/kw loops when the kernel is register-limited — this was the same anti-pattern that caused regressions in iterations 2, 3, and 4. The local load/store spill signature (1.0/32 bytes per sector) and 255 regs/thread are reliable indicators that the kernel is in a register-saturated regime where adding larger tiles will only worsen the situation.
framework_notes: In Triton, num_stages controls software pipelining depth. Reducing num_stages=1 removes pipeline buffering but does not reduce register pressure when the kernel body (via tl.static_range unrolling or large BLOCK_M) already demands 255 registers/thread. The key diagnostic: if registers/thread remains at 255 after applying num_stages=1, the pipeline stage count was not the source of register pressure. The diff also reintroduced tl.static_range for kh/kw loops (reverting from range()), which independently increases register demand. The autotuner selected BLOCK_M=256 with num_warps=8, which at 255 regs/thread saturates both Block Limit Registers (→1) and Block Limit Shared Mem (→1), leaving only 1 block per SM and 8 warps total — the minimum possible occupancy for this kernel.

strategy_title: Add num_stages=1 Autotune Configs to Reduce Shared Memory Pressure
strategy_description: When a Triton kernel's autotune configs exclusively use num_stages=2 or num_stages=3, the software pipelining allocates multiple shared memory buffers per block, which can severely limit Block Limit Shared Mem and reduce occupancy. Adding num_stages=1 configs to the autotune search space allows the autotuner to select a config that eliminates pipeline double/triple buffering, dramatically reducing dynamic shared memory per block (73.7 KB → 12.3 KB) and freeing Block Limit Shared Mem from 3 to 4. In this case, the autotuner selected a num_stages=1 config that also changed the loop structure from a flat K-loop to a triple nested kh/kw/in_c loop, which simultaneously halved the executed instruction count (1.68B → 0.95B) and tripled the L1/TEX hit rate (23% → 74%), producing a 1.28x speedup despite registers/thread remaining at 255 and occupancy unchanged at 12.5%.
slow_pseudocode:
# BEFORE: all autotune configs use num_stages=2 or num_stages=3
# num_stages=3 selected: 73.7 KB dynamic smem/block, Block Limit Shared Mem=3
@triton.autotune(configs=[
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 128, 'BLOCK_N': 64, 'BLOCK_K': 32}, num_stages=3, num_warps=4),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 128, 'BLOCK_N': 64, 'BLOCK_K': 16}, num_stages=2, num_warps=4),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 128, 'BLOCK_N': 32, 'BLOCK_K': 32}, num_stages=3, num_warps=4),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 64,  'BLOCK_N': 64, 'BLOCK_K': 32}, num_stages=3, num_warps=4),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 64,  'BLOCK_N': 64, 'BLOCK_K': 16}, num_stages=2, num_warps=4),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 64,  'BLOCK_N': 32, 'BLOCK_K': 32}, num_stages=3, num_warps=4),
], key=[...])
# Result: 73.7 KB smem/block, Block Limit Shared Mem=3, Duration=5.35ms
fast_pseudocode:
# AFTER: add num_stages=1 configs as primary candidates
# num_stages=1 selected: 12.3 KB dynamic smem/block, Block Limit Shared Mem=4
@triton.autotune(configs=[
    # num_stages=1: eliminates pipeline buffering smem overhead
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 128, 'BLOCK_N': 64, 'BLOCK_K': 16}, num_stages=1, num_warps=4),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 128, 'BLOCK_N': 32, 'BLOCK_K': 16}, num_stages=1, num_warps=4),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 64,  'BLOCK_N': 64, 'BLOCK_K': 16}, num_stages=1, num_warps=4),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 64,  'BLOCK_N': 32, 'BLOCK_K': 16}, num_stages=1, num_warps=4),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 128, 'BLOCK_N': 64, 'BLOCK_K': 32}, num_stages=1, num_warps=4),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 64,  'BLOCK_N': 64, 'BLOCK_K': 32}, num_stages=1, num_warps=4),
    # num_stages=2/3 fallbacks kept
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 128, 'BLOCK_N': 64, 'BLOCK_K': 16}, num_stages=2, num_warps=4),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 64,  'BLOCK_N': 64, 'BLOCK_K': 16}, num_stages=2, num_warps=4),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 64,  'BLOCK_N': 32, 'BLOCK_K': 16}, num_stages=2, num_warps=4),
    triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 128, 'BLOCK_N': 64, 'BLOCK_K': 32}, num_stages=3, num_warps=4),
], key=[...])
# Result: 12.3 KB smem/block, Block Limit Shared Mem=4, Duration=3.59ms
applicable_when: Triton kernel autotune configs exclusively use num_stages>=2, dynamic shared memory per block is large (>40 KB), Block Limit Shared Mem is the binding occupancy constraint (lower than Block Limit Registers or Block Limit Warps), and the L2 hit rate is high (>90%) indicating data is hot in cache so reduced pipeline depth will not hurt memory latency hiding. The TheoreticalOccupancy rule fires citing shared memory as a limiting factor.
do_not_apply_when: Do not add num_stages=1 configs when the kernel is memory-bandwidth-bound (DRAM throughput >60%) and relies on software pipelining to hide long DRAM latencies — reducing num_stages will expose those latencies and increase warp stall cycles. Also avoid when Block Limit Registers is already the binding constraint (not Block Limit Shared Mem), as reducing num_stages will not improve occupancy in that case.
framework_notes: In Triton, num_stages controls the software pipelining depth: num_stages=N allocates N sets of shared memory buffers for async prefetching. num_stages=3 with BLOCK_M=128, BLOCK_N=64, BLOCK_K=32 in fp32 requires approximately (128*32 + 32*64)*4*3 = 73 KB of shared memory per block. Reducing to num_stages=1 drops this to ~12 KB, freeing Block Limit Shared Mem from 3 to 4. The autotuner must be given num_stages=1 configs explicitly — it does not search this space automatically. Note that in this case the code diff also changed the loop structure (flat K-loop → nested kh/kw/in_c), so the L1 hit rate improvement (23% → 74%) and instruction count reduction (1.68B → 0.95B) may be partially attributable to the loop restructuring rather than num_stages alone.
